variants.name: Explicit loop (the portable realization)
variants.implementation_notes: Because no mainstream engine ships the specification's proper tail calls, the JavaScript realization of the pattern is the loop it stands for: reassign the accumulator-style parameters in a while/for loop and return from the base case. Default parameters, destructuring and for..of keep the state-carrying readable, and the function stays constant-stack on every engine. Treat the spec-mandated variant as an optimization that exists only on JavaScriptCore; anything that must run in Node, Chrome or Firefox has to be a loop.
pitfalls: Relying on proper tail calls throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded on V8 (Node, Chrome, Edge) and SpiderMonkey, because the elimination is specification text rather than shipped behaviour.
Even where it exists, PTC requires strict mode and a call in genuine tail position: wrapping it in Promise.resolve(), try/catch or a callback loses it silently.
Async code is never a tail call: an await before the recursive call stores a continuation on the heap, so depth moves from the stack into memory instead of disappearing.

variants.name: Spec-mandated proper tail calls (strict mode, JSC only)
variants.idiom_name: return f(...) in tail position under strict mode
variants.implementation_notes: The ECMAScript specification defines Tail Position Calls and PrepareForTailCall: in strict mode a call in tail position must discard the current execution context, so the recursion runs in constant stack. In practice only JavaScriptCore implements it; V8 shipped and then removed the feature and SpiderMonkey never shipped it. Keep this variant only for code that targets Safari/JavaScriptCore (or a host that embeds JSC) and keep the loop rewrite as the fallback everywhere else - the two produce identical results, only the stack profile differs.
pitfalls: The same function is a latent stack overflow on every engine except JavaScriptCore, so shipping it as the only path makes the depth bound engine-dependent.
The tail position is lost by the smallest change - a try block, a comma expression, a callback (forEach/map) around the call - and nothing warns.
Transpilation does not rescue it: Babel/TypeScript emit ordinary calls for tail-positioned recursion, so the spec behaviour survives only where the engine implements it.
